title: Chapter 9. Mettā (loving-kindness) (p. 31–45)

Ten Perfections Little · Children’s Books

Chapter 9. Mettā (loving-kindness) (p. 31–45)

Pages 31–45 (15 pages)
Page 31

Chapter 9. Mettā (loving-kindness) “Na maṃ koci uttasati, napi bhāyāmi kassaci; mettābalenupatthaddho, ramāmi pavane tadā”: No one was afraid of me, and I was afraid of no one. Held up by the power of loving-kindness, I was happy in the forest. (Cariyāpiṭaka 3.13) Mettā (loving-kindness1) means wishing others to be well and happy. All of them. Friends, and people who are not friends. People, and animals. When there is mettā (loving-kindness) in the mind, there is no anger in it at all. The Buddha said: as a mother would guard her only child with her own life, so let a mind of kindness go out to all beings2, without end. Sumedha’s picture. Sumedha thought of water. Water cools a good person and a bad person just the same. It washes the dust off both. Sumedha said: have mettā (loving-kindness) like that, the same for those who help and for those who harm. The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 31

Page 32

a good person a bad person water cools both the same and washes the dust off both mettā (loving-kindness) is the same for those who help and those who harm “Yathāpi udakaṃ nāma, kalyāṇe pāpake jane; samaṃ pharati sītena, pavāheti rajomalaṃ”: Like water, which cools good people and bad people just the same, and washes away dust and dirt. (Buddhavaṃsa 2) The story of Sāma. Once the Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be) was born as a boy named Sāma. His skin was golden, so people called him Suvaṇṇasāma, Golden Sāma. He lived in the forest with his mother and father, who were hermits3. When Sāma was small, an angry snake breathed poison into his parents’ eyes, and they both went blind. From then on Sāma looked after them. He brought them fruit. He fetched water from the river. He washed them, and he led them by the hand. Sāma was full of mettā (loving-kindness), and the animals of the forest felt it. Deer walked beside him. Lions and tigers did not hurt him. Nobody was afraid of him, and he was afraid of nobody. When he went to the river, the deer went with him, and he hung his water pots on a deer’s back. One day a king was hunting by the river. He saw a golden boy among the deer. He did not know what he was looking at. He shot an arrow with poison on it, and Sāma fell. Even then Sāma was not angry. He asked the king one thing: who will look after my blind mother and father now? The king was sorry. He went to the parents and told them what he had done. They did not hate the king. They came to their son, and they made an act of truth on his goodness. A goddess who lived in the forest did the same. The poison left Sāma’s body, and he stood up well. And his parents’ eyes could see again. Then Sāma taught the king, and the king went home and ruled kindly. Anna and the new girl. A new girl comes to Anna’s class. Nobody knows her. Anna smiles at her and shows her where to sit. That is mettā (loving-kindness). Real mettā (loving-kindness) is the same for a stranger as for a friend. That is how to tell that it is real. No one inside. Anna’s kindness is not Anna. It is mettā (loving-kindness), a good thing that comes up with a moment of mind, warms it, and goes. And the new girl is not one solid thing either. She is body and mind moments too, coming and going, just like Anna. There is no one inside Anna The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 32

Page 33

who loves, and no one inside the girl who is loved. There are moments of kindness, going out to a being who is also only moments. The Buddha taught that this is how it really is. HARD WORDS IN THIS CHAPTER 1. loving-kindness: wishing others well; friendliness to everyone 2. being: any living creature: a person, an animal, a heavenly being 3. hermit: a person who lives alone, away from other people The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 33

Chapter 10. Upekkhā (even-mindedness) “Ye me dukkhaṃ upaharanti, ye ca denti sukhaṃ mama; sabbesaṃ samako homi, dayā kopo na vijjati”: Those who gave me pain and those who gave me joy: to all of them I was the same. There was no favouring and no anger. (Cariyāpiṭaka 3.15) Upekkhā (even-mindedness1) means a mind that stays level. Winning does not lift it up. Losing does not throw it down. Praise and blame are both only sounds in the ear. The Buddha said: as a solid rock is not moved by the wind, so the wise are not moved by blame or by praise. Sumedha’s picture. Sumedha thought of the earth again. Clean things and dirty things are thrown on it. The earth does not love the one and hate the other. It is the same to both. Sumedha said: be like that in happiness and in pain, level, like a pair of scales. The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 34

Page 35

gain, praise, honour, happiness flowers, scented oils and food loss, blame, dishonour, misery spitting, jeering, grass in the ears upekkhā (even-mindedness) "I am impartial towards everything, and this is my perfection of equanimity." “Selo yathā ekaghano, vātena na samīrati; evaṃ nindāpasaṃsāsu, na samiñjanti paṇḍitā”: As a solid rock is not moved by the wind, so the wise are not moved by blame or praise. (Dhammapada 81) The story of the man who slept among the bones. Once the Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be) was a man who wanted to make upekkhā (even-mindedness) perfect. He went about in old clothes, and he let people think he was a fool. He came to a village and went to the burial ground. He lay down there, and he put a dead man’s bone under his head for a pillow. The village children found him. They were rough. They spat on him. They threw dirt at him. They poked grass into his ears and laughed at him. Other people came too, wise people. They were sorry for him. They brought him flowers and sweet-smelling oils and good food. He was the same to all of them. He was not angry with the children. He did not love the kind people more. He said afterwards that those who gave him pain and those who gave him joy were all the same to him. In pain and in happiness, in honour and in shame, he was like a pair of scales that stays level. Even-mindedness is not the same as not caring. The man among the bones cared about everyone. His mind was level, and it was kind. Anna comes last. There is a race. Anna comes last. Some children laugh. Anna’s face goes hot. Then she remembers the man among the bones. Coming last is only coming last. Laughing is only a sound. She smiles and goes to get a drink of water. That is a little upekkhā (even-mindedness). No one inside. A laugh is a sound. Hearing hears it. Then the hearing is gone. Then a thought comes: they are laughing at me. But there is no “me” in the sound, and no “me” in the hearing. When that is seen, the sound has nothing to hit. The mind stays level. Anna says: sabbe dhammā anattā (all things are not self). HARD WORDS IN THIS CHAPTER 1. even-mindedness: having a mind that stays level and calm whatever happens The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 36

Quiz 5 (chapters 9 and 10) The answers are at the back. 1. Who carried Sāma’s water pots to the river? (a) the king (b) a deer (c) his father 2. What was Sumedha’s picture for mettā (loving-kindness)? (a) water that cools good and bad people the same (b) fire (c) a yak 3. True or false: when the king shot him, Sāma was angry with the king. 4. What did the man among the bones use as a pillow? (a) a soft cushion (b) a dead man’s bone (c) a stone 5. How did the man among the bones feel about the rough children and the kind people? (a) angry with the children and glad with the kind people (b) the same to all of them (c) afraid of all of them 6. True or false: upekkhā (even-mindedness) means not caring about anyone. The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 37

Page 38

All ten together Sumedha found the ten. The Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be) made them perfect, life after life, for a time that nobody can count. Here they are, with Sumedha’s pictures and the stories. The perfection Sumedha’s picture The story dāna (giving) the full pot turned upside down the hare who gave himself sīla (good conduct) the yak that guards its tail the elephant who looked after his mother nekkhamma (letting go) the man who wants out of prison Prince Yudhañjaya and the dewdrops paññā (wisdom) the monk who goes to every house Mahosadha and the baby viriya (energy) the lion that is never slack Mahājanaka swimming in the sea khanti (patience) the earth that bears everything the buffalo and the monkey sacca (truthfulness) the morning star that keeps its path the little quail and the fire adhiṭṭhāna (determination) the mountain that no wind can move Prince Temiya, who did not speak mettā (loving-kindness) water that cools everyone the same Sāma and the deer upekkhā (evenmindedness) the earth that is the same to clean and dirty the man who slept among the bones In every story the Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be) was not thinking “I am the good one”. He was doing good. The ten are done by good moments of mind, one after another. Nobody owns them. And still they grow, and still they carry a person across the river. The Buddha said: if a person does good, let him do it again and again. Let him find joy in it. Happy is the piling up of good. And Anna says: sabbe dhammā anattā (all things are not self). Hard words Every hard English word in this book has a small number after it the first time it is met in a chapter, and its meaning is given at the end of that chapter. Here are all of them together, in alphabetical order. being: any living creature: a person, an animal, a heavenly being brahmin: a man of the priestly class in ancient India chariot: a cart with two wheels pulled by horses, used in old times for war and travel charioteer: the driver of a chariot deed: something done; an act, good or bad determination: making up one’s mind firmly and keeping to it energy: effort; the strength that keeps on going even-mindedness: having a mind that stays level and calm whatever happens hermit: a person who lives alone, away from other people ignorance: not knowing; not understanding what is really there lotus: a water flower that grows up from the mud and opens clean above the water loving-kindness: wishing others well; friendliness to everyone monk: a man who has left home to follow the Buddha’s rule of life nun: a woman who has left home to follow the Buddha’s rule of life perfection: a good quality made as full and strong as it can be suffering: pain and trouble; anything that cannot give lasting happiness truthfulness: always telling the truth and keeping to it The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 41

Page 42

Where the stories come from Everything in this book comes from the Tipiṭaka (the Three Baskets), the oldest collection of the Buddha’s teaching, and from the old commentaries that explain it. Nothing has been made up. The stories are told here in short, plain words for children, and the Pali lines under the pictures are given exactly as they stand in the old books, with a plain English rendering made for this book. Sumedha and the ten pictures. The Buddhavaṃsa (the Story of the Buddhas), chapter 2, the story of Sumedha. The ten pictures (the water pot, the yak, the prisoner, the monk, the lion, the earth, the morning star, the mountain, water, and the earth again) are Sumedha’s own, in that chapter. The commentaries say the time he took was four uncountable ages and a hundred thousand ages. The old teachers’ saying that a perfection is good conduct not spoilt by wanting, pride or the idea of a self comes from the commentary on the Cariyāpiṭaka (Basket of Conduct). The stories, by chapter. 1. The wise hare: Sasapaṇḍita Jātaka (birth story 316) and Cariyāpiṭaka 1.10. 2. The elephant who looked after his mother: Mātuposaka Jātaka (455) and Cariyāpiṭaka 2.1. 3. Prince Yudhañjaya: Yudhañjaya Jātaka (460) and Cariyāpiṭaka 3.1. 4. The boy Mahosadha and the baby: Mahā-ummagga Jātaka (546), among the cases he judged as a child of seven. 5. Prince Mahājanaka in the sea: Mahājanaka Jātaka (539). 6. The buffalo and the monkey: Mahiṃsa Jātaka (278) and Cariyāpiṭaka 2.5. 7. The little quail: Vaṭṭaka Jātaka (35) and Cariyāpiṭaka 3.9. 8. Prince Temiya: Mūgapakkha Jātaka (538) and Cariyāpiṭaka 3.6. 9. Sāma: Sāma Jātaka (540) and Cariyāpiṭaka 3.13. 10. The man who slept among the bones: Cariyāpiṭaka 3.15 and its commentary, with the Lomahaṃsa Jātaka (94). The cart. The nun Vajirā’s words about the cart and the person are in the Saṃyutta Nikāya (the Connected Sayings) 5.10. The Buddha’s words that a person who does not kill gives safety to all beings are in the Aṅguttara Nikāya (the Numbered Sayings), the Book of Eights. The lines under the pictures, and the Buddha’s words in the chapters. Dhammapada (the Verses of the Teaching) 81, 118, 184 and 279; Suttanipāta (the Collection of Discourses) 1.8 and 1.10; Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.80; Buddhavaṃsa chapter 2; the Jātaka verses of stories 35, 316, 455 and 539; and the Cariyāpiṭaka verses of the stories above. The Pali follows the Chaṭṭha Saṅgāyana text. The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 42

Answers Quiz 1 (chapters 1 and 2) 1. (c) his own body. The hare had only grass, so he gave himself. The fire did not burn him. 2. (a) a full pot turned upside down. The pot pours out all its water and keeps none back. 3. False. The fire felt cool to him, like cold water. 4. (b) he did not want to break his sīla (good conduct). He was strong enough to crush them, but fighting would have broken his good conduct. 5. (b) a yak that will not tear its tail. The yak would rather die than tear its tail. Good conduct is guarded like that. 6. True. When these two are in the mind, the rules are kept without any trouble. Quiz 2 (chapters 3 and 4) 1. (b) dewdrops drying up in the sun. The dewdrops were there, and then they were gone. He saw that everything is like that. 2. (a) a man who wants to get out of prison. The man in prison does not love the prison. He only looks for the way out. 3. False. He loved them. He only wanted something better than the kingdom: to become a Buddha. 4. (b) the real mother let go so that the baby would not be hurt. A mother’s heart is soft for her child. The yakkhinī (the wicked spirit) kept pulling. 5. (a) seven. He was seven years old, and already wise. 6. True. Like a lamp in a dark room, wisdom shows what is really there. Quiz 3 (chapters 5 and 6) 1. (b) seven. He swam for seven days, with no land in sight. 2. (b) a lion that is never slack. Sitting, standing or walking, the lion is never slack, and its mind is always awake. 3. False. He said he would go on striving, as far as he could and as hard as he could. 4. (a) kill the monkey. The spirit said one push with the horns would be enough. The buffalo did not do it. 5. (b) his sīla (good conduct) would break, and wise people would blame him. He said that if he were angry he would be lower than the monkey. 6. True. Patience burns away the dirt in the mind. Quiz 4 (chapters 7 and 8) The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 44

Page 45

1. (b) go back. He said that his wings could not fly, his feet could not walk, and his parents had gone. Then he told the fire to go back, and it did. 2. (a) the morning star that keeps its path. In every season the morning star keeps to its path. Truth is kept like that. 3. False. He may have broken other rules in some lives, but he never told a lie. 4. (b) sixteen. Sixteen years, and he never once let go of his plan. 5. (b) he stood up and lifted the chariot. He thought: now is my time. He stood up and lifted the chariot as a boy lifts a toy. 6. False. A wish is light and blows away. Determination is heavy, like a mountain. Quiz 5 (chapters 9 and 10) 1. (b) a deer. The deer walked with him because of his mettā (loving-kindness), and he hung the pots on a deer’s back. 2. (a) water that cools good and bad people the same. Water cools everyone the same and washes the dust off everyone. 3. False. He only asked who would look after his blind mother and father. 4. (b) a dead man’s bone. He lay in the burial ground with a bone for a pillow. 5. (b) the same to all of them. He said that those who gave him pain and those who gave him joy were all the same to him. 6. False. The man among the bones cared about everyone. His mind was level, and it was kind. The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 45
